meta.title: isotsbench · How expensive is crossing the TypeScript boundary?
meta.description: Cost profiles of calling native code from TypeScript across Node.js, Bun, Deno, scriptc, WebAssembly and browser Workers, from committed official benchmark runs.

hero.title: How expensive is crossing the TypeScript boundary?
hero.lede: A native function can be faster than JavaScript and still lose once you count the cost of calling it: entering native code, converting arguments, copying strings and buffers, building results. isotsbench measures that cost across runtimes, bindings, WebAssembly and browser Workers. It reports **cost profiles, not winners**.
hero.evidenceValue: 2 official runs, committed with every raw sample
hero.machineValue: Intel Core i7-12700H, Linux x86_64, turbo off, pinned CPUs

measured.title: What was measured
measured.lede: Synchronous microbenchmarks that isolate the boundary: no I/O, no database, no async. Every native path calls the same Rust core, and every result is checked against a TypeScript reference after timing.
measured.boundaryIsolates: the call itself, scalar conversion, break-even with work
measured.payloadIsolates: getting strings and buffers into native code
measured.returnIsolates: getting scalars, strings, buffers and row objects back
measured.pathsIntro: The path segment of a case id names what is measured: `op/path[/variant][/size]`, for example `sum_i32/wasm.copy/1000`. Paths with different semantics are never merged.
paths: `ts`: the TypeScript reference, JIT-compiled (compiled ahead of time under scriptc).
`napi`: a raw Node-API addon, the same file in Node.js, Bun and Deno.
`ffi`: a plain C ABI through `bun:ffi`, `Deno.dlopen` or scriptc's FFI.
`wasm.*`: WebAssembly without wasm-bindgen; suffixes name the call, the input and the build.
`worker.*`: a browser round trip to a dedicated Worker, suffixed by how the input moves.

targets.title: Targets
targets.lede: Four server runtimes, two browsers, and WebAssembly running inside both.
targets.wasmPaths: in Node.js, Bun, Deno and both browsers
gaps: scriptc has no JavaScript engine, so it has no Node-API; its FFI covers part of the matrix.
WebAssembly covers the boundary suite only; its payload and return paths are deferred.
Browsers have neither Node-API nor FFI, and run the boundary suite only.

glance.title: Results at a glance
glance.lede: Six observations from the official runs. Each links to the section with the measurements behind it.

items.claim: The call itself is small: nanoseconds, and the binding decides how many.
items.detail: In each runtime that has it, FFI was the cheapest real call; Node-API cost several times more, and most in Bun. In Node.js and Deno, V8 inlined a trivial WebAssembly call until nothing was left to measure.

items.claim: With enough work behind it, the binding stops mattering.
items.detail: Over a million elements, every Node-API and FFI sum took about the same time, whatever its call cost.

items.claim: Data shape matters more than JS vs native.
items.detail: ASCII strings cross cheaply; through Node-API, mixed UTF-8 never beat TypeScript in Node.js or Deno. Returning rows as JavaScript objects through Node-API was slower than building them in TypeScript at every measured size.

items.claim: WebAssembly pays for transfer and for code generation.
items.detail: Copying input into linear memory and the default build's scalar code each account for a comparable share of the gap to native. With `simd128` and resident input, WebAssembly comes close to native.

items.claim: A Worker round trip costs microseconds before any data moves.
items.detail: That is thousands of times a main-thread call. For large inputs, how the input reaches the Worker matters more than what runs there.

items.claim: V8's JIT history can change a result several times over.
items.detail: The same TypeScript loop can run several times slower in a fresh process than in one that ran other cases first. Both are measured and reported, never averaged.

boundary.title: Boundary cost
boundary.lede: The cost of a call with no work and no data, `noop`, is the floor for each binding. The TypeScript `noop` is inlined into an empty loop, so here the absolute native time matters, not a ratio against TypeScript.
points: FFI and a real WebAssembly call cost a few nanoseconds; Node-API cost more, and how much depended strongly on the runtime.

Work proportional to the input, as in `sum_i32`, eventually hides the crossing. The **break-even size** is the smallest measured size from which native beats that runtime's TypeScript at every larger size.
Scalar arguments add conversion cost on some paths, such as scriptc's `add_i32`.

dataShape.title: Data shape matters more than JS vs native
dataShape.lede: Whether native code wins depends less on the language behind the boundary than on what crosses it: a borrowed buffer, a one-byte string, a two-byte string, a new buffer, or one JavaScript object per row.

patterns.title: Borrowed native computation
patterns.measured: Handing a buffer to Node-API or FFI took about the same time at 16 B and at 16 MiB: across all six sizes, no path's time varied by more than {borrowed}.
patterns.implication: Pass buffers as they are, and give native code the whole job in one call. Handing over a borrowed buffer costs the same at any size, so the number of calls adds up, not the amount of data.

patterns.title: Copying an array into WebAssembly linear memory
patterns.measured: At 10⁶ elements the copy alone took {copy} per call, while the whole native sum took {native}.
patterns.implication: Keep the data WebAssembly works on in linear memory, and copy it in once. An API that takes a new JavaScript array on every call pays for the copy every time.

patterns.title: Returning a large byte buffer
patterns.code:
// Native code allocates and fills one buffer; JS receives a single Uint8Array.
const image = native.render(width, height);   // 16 MiB, one object
patterns.measured: Returning a new 16 MiB buffer through Node-API was {bytesOut} faster than filling one in TypeScript, across runtimes and both process modes.
patterns.implication: Return bulk results as one typed array or buffer. Small results behave differently: a new 16-byte buffer cost more through Node-API than in TypeScript in Node.js and Bun.

patterns.title: Returning thousands of JavaScript objects
patterns.measured: Returning 10,000 rows as objects through Node-API took {objects} as long as building them in TypeScript; packed records decoded in JavaScript took {packed}. No native row strategy beat TypeScript at any measured size, from 1 to 10,000 rows.
patterns.implication: Many small JavaScript objects were the most expensive shape measured, and a packed buffer reduced that cost without beating TypeScript. Where rows must become JavaScript objects, building them in TypeScript was faster here; otherwise, keep them on the native side and return only what the caller needs.

dataShape.deeper: How each binding copies, borrows or allocates: [marshalling.md](https://github.com/gilvandovieira/isotsbench/blob/main/docs/marshalling.md).

wasm.title: WebAssembly: transfer and code generation
wasm.lede: Node-API and FFI borrow the caller's array; WebAssembly must first copy it into linear memory. Its penalty is that copy plus the code the default build generates, and the two are measured apart.
points: `wasm.copy` copies the input on every call; `wasm.resident` copies it once, outside timing. Their difference is the transfer.
The default build's sum is scalar, while native Rust is auto-vectorised. `simd128` is the same source built with SIMD, as a separate path.
`wasm.inlineable` is the engine's default call, which V8 may inline away; `wasm.no-inline` measures the call with inlining disabled.

workers.title: Workers: a messaging boundary
workers.lede: A Worker round trip is a messaging boundary, not a WebAssembly one. It is measured as sequential round trips, main thread → Worker → main thread, separately for each way of moving the input.
points: `clone`: `postMessage` copies the array; the caller keeps it.
`copy`: the caller copies with `slice()` and transfers the copy.
`transfer`: the caller's buffer moves to the Worker and back.
`resident`: the input already lives in the Worker; no data moves.
WebAssembly in a Worker always copies the received array into linear memory, so even a transfer pays for one copy.
workers.caveat: These are latencies of one request at a time. They do not measure keeping the main thread free, or throughput with several messages in flight.

jit.title: Fresh vs shared: JIT history
jit.lede: Every case runs twice per run: in a fresh process (or browser), and in one shared process per runtime (or page per browser and thread) after the cases before it. The same case can differ several times over between the two.
points: Differences of several times appeared only in V8 (Node.js, Deno, Chromium), in both directions. Bun and Firefox diverged too, but far less.
scriptc compiles ahead of time and has no JIT: its fresh and shared processes run the same machine code, and their results stayed close.
The harness never works around this with engine flags or by reshaping loops. Neither mode is the right answer, so both are published.

methodology.title: Methodology and caveats
methodology.lede: Results are only comparable when they were measured the same way, so the method is part of every result.
points: **Batched timing.** Batches calibrated to about 20 ms; 5 warmup batches, then 30 measured. Raw samples are kept.
**Three runs, shuffled.** A seeded shuffle orders every unit across runtimes, cases and modes; the seed is recorded.
**Correctness after timing.** Each process checks what it measured against the TypeScript reference after measuring. A mismatch discards the unit.
**Official conditions.** `performance` governor, turbo off, pinned CPUs, no condition warnings, no failed units.
reading: A value is the median of three per-run medians.
When fresh and shared results diverge (their per-run medians do not overlap and differ by more than 5%), both are shown.
When a case's per-run medians spread more than 5%, its range is shown instead of one number.
Ratios compare paths inside one runtime. Absolute times from different runtimes share the machine, not the engine.
caveats: One machine, one platform: an i7-12700H laptop on Linux x86_64. macOS, Windows, Safari and mobile are not covered.
Some cases remain unstable between runs. The 5% threshold is a heuristic; there are no confidence intervals yet.
Microbenchmarks only, all synchronous. Async calls, chatty vs batched APIs and a realistic SQLite workload are planned.
The repository also documents development runs (turbo on). Never compare their absolute times with these.
claims: That native code is always faster than TypeScript.
That one runtime is faster than another, or that FFI always beats Node-API.
That WebAssembly is equivalent to native code.
That a microbenchmark represents application performance.

evidence.title: Evidence and data
evidence.lede: The repository and its committed runs are the source of truth. This page is a reading of them.
evidence.rawRuntimes: Node.js, Bun, Deno and scriptc; every suite.
evidence.rawBrowsers: Chromium and Firefox; main thread and Worker.
evidence.rawNote: Each directory holds `environment.json` (hardware, versions, conditions, artifact hashes, seed) and one file per runtime or browser thread with every raw sample.
evidence.normalizedText: `results.json`, `results.csv` and `metadata.json`: one record per run, environment, isolation mode and case, each traced to its raw record. Regenerated by `make normalize`.
evidence.reproduceNote: Linux only. `make setup` changes CPU settings through `sudo`; `make teardown` restores them.

boundary.title: Cost of one empty call
boundary.reading: An FFI call cost {ffi} and a Node-API call {napi}, depending on the runtime. In Node.js and Deno the default WebAssembly call cost exactly what the empty loop cost: no call was left to measure. With inlining turned off it cost {noInline}.
boundary.description: Time per `noop` call, by path, grouped by runtime.

wasmSum.title: Summing 10⁶ integers: native and WebAssembly
wasmSum.reading: Every native path took {native}. The default WebAssembly build was slower even with its input already in linear memory ({resident}). Built with `simd128`, the resident sum came within {simd} of Node-API.
wasmSum.description: `sum_i32` over 10⁶ elements, per call, in each server runtime and browser main thread.

wasmSplit.title: Where WebAssembly's time goes
wasmSplit.reading: Copying 10⁶ integers into linear memory added {transfer} per call: more than the whole native sum. The `simd128` build shortened the sum, not the copy.
wasmSplit.description: Each bar is `wasm.copy`, split into the sum on resident input (`wasm.resident`) and the remainder, the copy. The split subtracts two independently measured medians, so it is approximate. Fresh processes; the tick marks the native Node-API sum.

workers.title: Worker round trips by how the input moves
workers.reading: A round trip with no data cost {trip}. With 10⁶ elements, moving the input to the Worker added about {transfer} with a transfer, {copy} with an explicit copy and {clone} with a structured clone, compared with input already there.
workers.description: Sequential round trips, main thread → Worker → main thread, with `sum_i32` in WebAssembly inside the Worker. The last row of each browser is the same sum on its main thread.

jit.title: The same code, fresh and shared
jit.reading: Node.js ran the same TypeScript sum {node} faster in a shared process than in a fresh one. Deno's checksum went the other way: {deno} slower in a shared process. scriptc, which has no JIT, and Bun, whose engine is JavaScriptCore, showed no such difference for the sum.
jit.description: Two of the cases where fresh and shared results diverge, and two controls. Shared processes ran other cases first.

dataShape.title: Node-API time relative to TypeScript, by what crosses
dataShape.reading: ASCII strings in and new buffers out sit left of the line in every runtime: Node-API was faster. Rows returned as objects sit far to the right, and packed rows close only part of that gap.
dataShape.description: Node-API time divided by TypeScript time in the same runtime. Left of the line, Node-API was faster.
